prep.video2:
Game development requires a positive mindset because it encourages creativity, perseverance, adaptability, collaboration, and customer focus. Developers need creativity to come up with new ideas, perseverance to overcome challenges, and adaptability to keep up with changing technology. Collaboration is important because programmers, artists, and designers must work together. Developers must also consider the players' needs to create enjoyable games.

A growth mindset means believing that your abilities can improve through effort and learning. Developers can develop this mindset by embracing challenges, learning from mistakes, focusing on effort, accepting feedback, finding positive role models, and continuously learning new skills. Instead of viewing failure as something negative, they should treat it as an opportunity to improve.

Some common obstacles in game development include technical problems, scope creep, marketing, funding, and burnout. Technical problems can be addressed through testing, teamwork, and documentation. Scope creep happens when developers continually add features beyond the original plan, which can cause delays and complications. Developers should establish clear goals and stick to their plans. Marketing and distribution require understanding the target audience, while funding can be addressed through business plans, grants, and crowdfunding. Burnout can be prevented by taking breaks, maintaining balance, and seeking support.

To stay motivated and focused, developers should set manageable goals, celebrate small achievements, take regular breaks, stay organized, and remain passionate about their projects. Communication and collaboration also help teams solve problems and stay on track. Overall, successful game development requires patience, organization, teamwork, creativity, and a willingness to learn from mistakes.
prep.video3: A well-organized folder structure is important in game development because it makes projects easier to manage, improves efficiency, and helps individuals or teams find files quickly. Before starting a project, developers should plan how folders and files will be named, organized, stored, and backed up. Keeping a project log is also useful because it records the dates, times, and progress made throughout development. Developers can manually create folders and files or use a JSON-based application to automatically generate them. JSON allows users to define folder names, file types, and file contents, making project setup faster and easier. A game development folder structure may include folders for context, requirements, resources, assets, models, exports, and study materials, with README files explaining what each folder contains. A Game Development Document (GDD) also serves as a blueprint for the project by organizing its concept, backstory, requirements, and other important information. Overall, planning and maintaining an organized file structure helps developers stay efficient, collaborate effectively, and prepare for future stages of game development.
prep.video4: This video provides a guide on setting up and maintaining documentation for game development projects. The creator explains the importance of using a well-structured game development document as a blueprint for team communication and project organization. The tutorial demonstrates how to customize templates by updating titles, subtitles, and imagery, while also highlighting the need to include sections for game overviews, backstories, milestones, and task assignments. Additionally, the video covers best practices for folder structures, such as creating dedicated areas for project assets, resources like software and documentation, and onboarding materials for new team members. By organizing these files and documents effectively, developers can streamline their workflow, from initial setup and asset gathering to programming, testing, and final publication.
prep.video5: This video serves as an introductory guide to setting up a *Unity* project for the game *Tale of the Temper*. The creator emphasizes the importance of proper file management by demonstrating how to use a simplified file path to avoid common errors during project decompression. After creating the project using the *Third Person Core* template, the video provides a walkthrough of the *Unity IDE*, detailing essential tabs such as the *Hierarchy*, *Scene View*, *Game View*, *Inspector*, and *Project* view. The creator also teaches fundamental navigation techniques using the mouse and shortcut keys, and concludes by testing the template's default character movement, noting that the next video will focus on replacing this default model with a custom character to personalize the game.
prep.video6: In this video, the creator guides viewers through the process of importing and setting up a custom character in a Unity project. The process begins with establishing an organized folder structure using the Tolstra Json Folder and File Maker, followed by importing a downloaded 3D character mesh into the project. The creator explains how to configure the character's rig as humanoid and apply its materials, then demonstrates how to replace the original template character with the new one by unpacking the prefab and swapping the avatar. The tutorial concludes with tips on duplicating objects like boxes and ground meshes to expand the game environment.

huddle.tech:
Engine: Unity. It’s free, lightweight, and has good beginner tutorials, so everyone can install it and start quickly.

Language: Unity C#. It’s built into Godot and easy to read, so teammates can understand each other’s code.

Packages/add-ons: Godot’s built-in 2D/3D tools (sprites, collision, UI nodes) so we don’t depend on extra downloads that might break.

Assets: Free, license-friendly art and sound (for example from Kenney.nl or OpenGameArt), plus our own wanted-poster designs made in Canva or Figma. We chose free assets so we don’t have copyright problems.

Who checks them:

[Leah Aluni] checks that the engine and code run on every team member’s computer.
[Nicolas Kuhnast] checks that every asset has a license that lets us use it.
[George Arbache] tests the finished build after each change.

Why we chose these: They’re free, beginner-friendly, and work well for a small team with limited time. Open question: Do we need any extra add-ons for saving scores, or is the built-in system enough? I used Claude to get the answer
huddle.code:
Start / Update
Callback | What happens | Verified
Awake() | Sets up references (player, bounty list) before the game starts | [x]
Start() | Loads the first bounty and sets the score to 0 | [x]
Update() | Every frame: reads player input, moves the player, checks if the bounty is caught | [x]
OnCollisionEnter2D() | Runs when the player touches a bounty target, then adds the reward to the score | [x]

Classes & components
Class | Responsibility | GameObject
PlayerController | Reads input and moves the player; checks when the player touches a bounty | Player
BountyTarget | Stores each target’s name, difficulty, and reward value | Bounty (prefab)
GameManager | Tracks the score and which bounty is active; decides when the game ends | GameManager (empty object)
UIManager | Updates the score text and shows the win or game over screen | Canvas

Packages / using
Package / namespace | Why included | Tested
using UnityEngine; | Gives access to the core engine tools our scripts need, like MonoBehaviour, Transform, Input, and Vector2 | [x]
using UnityEngine.UI; | Lets us update the score text and buttons on the screen from code | [x]
using System.Collections.Generic; | Lets us use List<> to store the bounty list and loop through it | [x]
using UnityEngine.SceneManagement; | Lets us reload the scene when the player restarts after winning or losing | [x]

huddle.reuse:
PlayerController script (our own code). Source: written by our team. Credit: none required, but we’ll keep our names in the code comments.
GameManager and score system (our own code). Source: written by our team. Credit: none required. It can be reused for any game that tracks points or objectives.
Bounty data structure (BountyTarget class). Source: our team. Credit: none required. We can swap in new characters, rewards, and difficulty levels for a new story.
Free art and sound assets (for example from Kenney.nl or OpenGameArt). Source: the website and creator’s name, saved in a credits file. Credit: we’ll check each license, since some (CC0) need no credit and others (CC-BY) require us to name the creator.
Our wanted-poster and menu designs (Canva or Figma). Source: our team. Credit: if we used Canva templates or stock elements, we’ll check Canva’s license terms before reusing them. I used Claude for my answer.
huddle.boardNotes:
What the huddle board is: A shared space where our team writes down what we discussed, what we agreed on, and what we still need to figure out, so nobody has to rely on memory and everyone can see the same plan.

Decisions we made:

We will build the game in [Godot/Unity] using [GDScript/C#], because it’s free and beginner-friendly.
We will keep the game small: at least 3 bounties, a score system, and a win or game over screen.
We will use free, license-friendly assets and keep a credits file listing each source.
Each person owns one part of the pipeline: [Name 1] inputs, [Name 2] building, [Name 3] design, [Name 4] testing.

Disagreements:

Some of us wanted more bounties and extra levels, while others wanted to finish a smaller game that works. We agreed to finish 3 bounties first and add more only if time is left.
We discussed whether to draw our own art or use free assets. We chose free assets for the characters and made our own wanted posters.

Questions that remain open:

Do we need an extra add-on to save high scores, or is the built-in system enough?
Who will double-check that every asset’s license allows us to reuse it?
How many classmates can test the game before the deadline? I used Claude to get the answers

board.notes:
Our mission is to build a playable bounty hunting game with at least three bounties, a score system, and a win or game over screen. In our huddle we compared our ideas for the mission and agreed to keep the game small so we can finish it.

The diagram shows the mission at the top, connected to three jobs. [Name 1] builds the game and scoring. [Name 2] designs the posters, menus, and art. [Name 3] tests the game, keeps the bug list, and checks that every asset’s license lets us use it. All three jobs lead to the finished prototype at the bottom.

We decided that each person owns one job so nothing is missed, and that we will check in again before the deadline. One disagreement was whether to add more bounties or finish a smaller game first, and we chose to finish three bounties first. One open question is how we will save high scores. we used claude to get the answers

prep.video2:
Game development requires a positive mindset because it encourages creativity, perseverance, adaptability, collaboration, and customer focus. Developers need creativity to come up with new ideas, perseverance to overcome challenges, and adaptability to keep up with changing technology. Collaboration is important because programmers, artists, and designers must work together. Developers must also consider the players' needs to create enjoyable games.

A growth mindset means believing that your abilities can improve through effort and learning. Developers can develop this mindset by embracing challenges, learning from mistakes, focusing on effort, accepting feedback, finding positive role models, and continuously learning new skills. Instead of viewing failure as something negative, they should treat it as an opportunity to improve.

Some common obstacles in game development include technical problems, scope creep, marketing, funding, and burnout. Technical problems can be addressed through testing, teamwork, and documentation. Scope creep happens when developers continually add features beyond the original plan, which can cause delays and complications. Developers should establish clear goals and stick to their plans. Marketing and distribution require understanding the target audience, while funding can be addressed through business plans, grants, and crowdfunding. Burnout can be prevented by taking breaks, maintaining balance, and seeking support.

To stay motivated and focused, developers should set manageable goals, celebrate small achievements, take regular breaks, stay organized, and remain passionate about their projects. Communication and collaboration also help teams solve problems and stay on track. Overall, successful game development requires patience, organization, teamwork, creativity, and a willingness to learn from mistakes.
prep.video3: A well-organized folder structure is important in game development because it makes projects easier to manage, improves efficiency, and helps individuals or teams find files quickly. Before starting a project, developers should plan how folders and files will be named, organized, stored, and backed up. Keeping a project log is also useful because it records the dates, times, and progress made throughout development. Developers can manually create folders and files or use a JSON-based application to automatically generate them. JSON allows users to define folder names, file types, and file contents, making project setup faster and easier. A game development folder structure may include folders for context, requirements, resources, assets, models, exports, and study materials, with README files explaining what each folder contains. A Game Development Document (GDD) also serves as a blueprint for the project by organizing its concept, backstory, requirements, and other important information. Overall, planning and maintaining an organized file structure helps developers stay efficient, collaborate effectively, and prepare for future stages of game development.
prep.video4: This video provides a guide on setting up and maintaining documentation for game development projects. The creator explains the importance of using a well-structured game development document as a blueprint for team communication and project organization. The tutorial demonstrates how to customize templates by updating titles, subtitles, and imagery, while also highlighting the need to include sections for game overviews, backstories, milestones, and task assignments. Additionally, the video covers best practices for folder structures, such as creating dedicated areas for project assets, resources like software and documentation, and onboarding materials for new team members. By organizing these files and documents effectively, developers can streamline their workflow, from initial setup and asset gathering to programming, testing, and final publication.
prep.video5: This video serves as an introductory guide to setting up a *Unity* project for the game *Tale of the Temper*. The creator emphasizes the importance of proper file management by demonstrating how to use a simplified file path to avoid common errors during project decompression. After creating the project using the *Third Person Core* template, the video provides a walkthrough of the *Unity IDE*, detailing essential tabs such as the *Hierarchy*, *Scene View*, *Game View*, *Inspector*, and *Project* view. The creator also teaches fundamental navigation techniques using the mouse and shortcut keys, and concludes by testing the template's default character movement, noting that the next video will focus on replacing this default model with a custom character to personalize the game.
prep.video6: In this video, the creator guides viewers through the process of importing and setting up a custom character in a Unity project. The process begins with establishing an organized folder structure using the Tolstra Json Folder and File Maker, followed by importing a downloaded 3D character mesh into the project. The creator explains how to configure the character's rig as humanoid and apply its materials, then demonstrates how to replace the original template character with the new one by unpacking the prefab and swapping the avatar. The tutorial concludes with tips on duplicating objects like boxes and ground meshes to expand the game environment.

huddle.tech:
Engine: Unity. It’s free, lightweight, and has good beginner tutorials, so everyone can install it and start quickly.

Language: Unity C#. It’s built into Godot and easy to read, so teammates can understand each other’s code.

Packages/add-ons: Godot’s built-in 2D/3D tools (sprites, collision, UI nodes) so we don’t depend on extra downloads that might break.

Assets: Free, license-friendly art and sound (for example from Kenney.nl or OpenGameArt), plus our own wanted-poster designs made in Canva or Figma. We chose free assets so we don’t have copyright problems.

Who checks them:

[Leah Aluni] checks that the engine and code run on every team member’s computer.
[Nicolas Kuhnast] checks that every asset has a license that lets us use it.
[George Arbache] tests the finished build after each change.

Why we chose these: They’re free, beginner-friendly, and work well for a small team with limited time. Open question: Do we need any extra add-ons for saving scores, or is the built-in system enough? I used Claude to get the answer

huddle.reuse:
PlayerController script (our own code). Source: written by our team. Credit: none required, but we’ll keep our names in the code comments.
GameManager and score system (our own code). Source: written by our team. Credit: none required. It can be reused for any game that tracks points or objectives.
Bounty data structure (BountyTarget class). Source: our team. Credit: none required. We can swap in new characters, rewards, and difficulty levels for a new story.
Free art and sound assets (for example from Kenney.nl or OpenGameArt). Source: the website and creator’s name, saved in a credits file. Credit: we’ll check each license, since some (CC0) need no credit and others (CC-BY) require us to name the creator.
Our wanted-poster and menu designs (Canva or Figma). Source: our team. Credit: if we used Canva templates or stock elements, we’ll check Canva’s license terms before reusing them. I used Claude for my answer.
huddle.boardNotes:
What the huddle board is: A shared space where our team writes down what we discussed, what we agreed on, and what we still need to figure out, so nobody has to rely on memory and everyone can see the same plan.

Decisions we made:

We will build the game in [Godot/Unity] using [GDScript/C#], because it’s free and beginner-friendly.
We will keep the game small: at least 3 bounties, a score system, and a win or game over screen.
We will use free, license-friendly assets and keep a credits file listing each source.
Each person owns one part of the pipeline: [Name 1] inputs, [Name 2] building, [Name 3] design, [Name 4] testing.

Disagreements:

Some of us wanted more bounties and extra levels, while others wanted to finish a smaller game that works. We agreed to finish 3 bounties first and add more only if time is left.
We discussed whether to draw our own art or use free assets. We chose free assets for the characters and made our own wanted posters.

Questions that remain open:

Do we need an extra add-on to save high scores, or is the built-in system enough?
Who will double-check that every asset’s license allows us to reuse it?
How many classmates can test the game before the deadline? I used Claude to get the answers
